title: Why Genomic Computation?
scope: Next execution writes this chapter; this milestone creates no manuscript, finished artwork or animation frames.
sizePolicy: Let the argument determine length; a substantial 30–50-page treatment is acceptable, not a quota. The opening establishes the field and exact worked mechanisms without duplicating later full treatments.

sections.title: Programs, neural models and genomes
sections.purpose: Begin with the real comparison: what is stored, selected, executed, persistent and changed? Ordinary software and neural systems can already be conditional; cells need molecular machinery, not DNA alone.
sections.formalism: Use separate typed lanes before a shared abstraction. A neural parameter tensor, a program and a physical genome are not interchangeable objects.
sections.workedExample: Compare a compiled program with dispatch, a conditional neural model and a regulated biological system; annotate where the analogy breaks.

sections.title: Stored structure versus expressed computation
sections.purpose: Use a concrete library of computational modules and a context-dependent selection. Define the execution plan as a selected computation, not just a list of names.
sections.formalism: Provisional P_x=Reg(G,x), (y,Ω)=Exec(P_x,x); define G, x, plan type, y and trace Ω. Stateful cases require an explicit state argument.
sections.workedExample: Work a small deterministic two-module routing example with exact inputs, selected plan, output and trace; show a conventional implementation produces the same behavior.

sections.title: Regulation and expression as mechanisms
sections.purpose: Explain what controls selection and what operation becomes active. Compare if/else, dispatch, gates, mixture of experts, attention and query planning at mechanism level; defer model internals to Part II.
sections.formalism: Give domain/codomain and cost for the selector and executor. An ordinary dispatch equivalence is a useful negative result.
sections.workedExample: Trace two contexts through the same stored catalog; show changed selection without changing the catalog or claiming learning.

sections.title: Development, learning, adaptation and evolution
sections.purpose: Separate runtime state, learned parameters, generated structure and population change. Illustrate development as building a computational phenotype without claiming it is biological development.
sections.formalism: Candidate P=Dev(G,E); specify environment E and generated program P. Distinguish s_t, θ, structure and population as different changing objects.
sections.workedExample: Classify four updates by object, timescale, objective and inheritance; explain that relative timescales are design choices rather than universal laws.

sections.purpose: Make the nearest baselines central: conditional execution, MoE, recurrent state, compilation, neural architecture search, evolutionary computation, query optimization and orchestration.
sections.formalism: Separate representational novelty from algorithmic novelty, expressivity, efficiency and measurable utility.
sections.workedExample: Construct a comparison table where a proposal is equivalent to dispatch, then state what additional semantics or evidence would be needed for a stronger claim.

sections.title: A research thesis with a falsifiable gap
sections.purpose: Frame Evolutor as investigation of selection, composition, development and adaptation across heterogeneous computation. Start with mechanisms; keep full provenance and repeated caveats in ledgers.
sections.formalism: Introduce a candidate cost vector for storage, regulation, execution, state, trace and adaptation; defer its formal complexity treatment.
sections.workedExample: Ask whether a proposed selective transformation improves a declared task at matched total resources; specify the result that would reject the proposal.

sections.title: DOGMA and Hermon DNA: two architecture families
sections.purpose: DOGMA is the non-Transformer DNA-native research line, not merely an RNN with biological names. Hermon DNA is the Transformer-based DNA line. Explain carried state versus attention-accessible cached representations as a first systems distinction.
sections.formalism: Candidate DOGMA (x_t,s_t)↦(s_{t+1},y_t), with prediction timing declared. Hermon consumes token x_t with prior cache and appends K/V for that token. No off-by-one cache convention.
sections.workedExample: Compare what persists in each family; bounded carried state does not imply infinite recall or constant total memory. Attention access does not guarantee exact retrieval.

sections.title: From theory to reference models, engines and runtime
sections.purpose: Show theory, model architecture, training, engine execution, orchestration and industrial serving as separate levels. Evolutor sits above DOGMA Engine and Hermon DNA Engine and may compose other modules.
sections.formalism: Define reference → parity → profile → optimization as engineering gates, not performance claims. Formal semantics and full model mathematics come later.
sections.workedExample: Give a concrete next-step research contract with baseline, implementation, tests and limits; provide technical conceptual and design exercises rather than syntax drills.

exercisePolicy: Include a fully solved technical example, derivation, algorithm or proof task, implementation check, experimental/systems design task and research critique. Open problems get a rubric, not fabricated solutions.
codePlan: Implement a small deterministic selection/execution/trace example and conventional baseline, with exact tests. It is an analogy experiment, not a DOGMA model, Transformer, training library or engine.
acceptance: Chapter starts with the actual subject, not counters or a thermostat.
Definitions and abstraction boundaries are explicit; useful abstraction is not prohibited.
Every displayed formula has defined symbols, assumptions and interpretation.
Every figure has editable source and a Unicode TXT companion; scientific and final-page reviews remain required.
No novelty, performance, biomedical or AGI conclusion without corresponding evidence.
